report:
**Conclusion: supported.** High-quality randomized evidence shows that the two-dose adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV; Shingrix) substantially reduces shingles in immunocompetent adults aged 70 years or older.

The pivotal ZOE-70 trial was randomized and placebo-controlled. It found vaccine efficacy of **89.8%** against confirmed herpes zoster (95% CI 84.2%–93.7%) in adults ≥70, with comparable estimates in those 70–79 (90.0%) and ≥80 (89.1%). This directly tests the claim and makes confounding unlikely.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27626517/  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/10.1056/NEJMoa1603800?page=2

Evidence is also consistent across the broader phase-3 program: the related ≥50-year trial found a 97.2% lower shingles risk versus placebo, and later summaries report >90% efficacy in the pivotal trials.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33606577/?dopt=Abstract

**Important qualifications:** “Reduces” does not mean eliminates risk; effectiveness can be lower outside trials than efficacy under trial conditions, and protection depends on receiving the recommended two-dose series. The pivotal population was principally healthy/immunocompetent older adults, so the exact estimate should not automatically be applied to every medically complex or immunocompromised person. The vaccine also commonly causes short-lived injection-site and systemic reactions; its benefits should be assessed alongside those harms rather than treating it as risk-free. A 2023 Cochrane review concludes vaccines prevent shingles in healthy older adults, but rates the overall evidence as moderate certainty and notes that the evidence base is in older adult study populations.  
https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD008858_vaccines-preventing-shingles-older-adults
